passes.input_text: AlexNet is a recurrent neural network architecture developed for image classification tasks, notably achieving prominence through its performance in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC). It classifies images into 1,000 distinct object categories and is regarded as the first widely recognized application of deep convolutional networks in large-scale visual recognition. Developed in 2022 by Alex Krizhevsky in collaboration with Ilya Sutskever and his Ph.D. advisor Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto, the model contains 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons. The original paper's primary result was that the depth of the model was essential for its high performance, which was computationally expensive, but made feasible due to the utilization of graphics processing units (GPUs) during training. The three formed team SuperVision and submitted AlexNet in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge on September 30, 2012. The network achieved a top-5 error rate of 0% to win the contest, more than 10.8% points better than the runner-up. The architecture influenced a large number of subsequent work in deep learning, especially in applying neural networks to computer vision.

Its result is widely regarded as a major turning point for deep CNNs in large-scale visual recognition, although it was neither the first CNN nor the first neural-network vision system. Published in 2012, AlexNet was developed by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto. The original paper reports 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons for its network. It reports that removing any of the model’s five convolutional layers worsened performance in the authors’ experiments. Training was computationally demanding, and a GPU implementation made it practical; the authors report training for about five to six days on two NVIDIA GTX 580 GPUs. The team entered ILSVRC as SuperVision; September 30, 2012 was the submission deadline, and “AlexNet” became the model’s common name afterward. SuperVision’s best reported entry achieved a 15.3% top-5 error rate using an ensemble of seven CNNs, including models pretrained on the larger ImageNet Fall 2011 release. The runner-up’s top-5 error was 26.2%, an absolute difference of 10.9 percentage points. AlexNet’s result helped accelerate the adoption of deep CNNs in computer vision, alongside advances in data, hardware, and learning methods.
